description: A study of how colonial powers reorganised the economy of Tanganyika and East Africa through cash-crop agriculture, mining, infrastructure, forced and migrant labour, taxation and land alienation, and the effects of these on Africans.

mcq.questionText: What was the MAIN aim of the colonial economy in Tanganyika and East Africa?

options.text: To develop African industries for local use
To serve the economic interests of the colonising country
To make Africans self-sufficient in food production
To promote equal trade between Africa and Europe

mcq.explanation: The colonial economy was designed mainly to supply raw materials and markets that benefited the metropolitan (colonising) country, not the colonised people.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a type of cash-crop agriculture used in the colonial economy?

options.text: Subsistence farming
Shifting cultivation
Plantation agriculture
Nomadic pastoralism

mcq.explanation: Plantation agriculture, along with settler and peasant farming, was one of the main forms of cash-crop production in the colonial economy.

mcq.questionText: In a plantation economy, who mainly owned and controlled the large estates?

options.text: African peasant farmers
Foreign companies and European individuals
Local African chiefs
Asian traders only

mcq.explanation: Plantations were large estates owned by foreign companies or European individuals who employed cheap African labour to grow crops such as sisal.

mcq.questionText: Which cash crop was most associated with plantation agriculture in colonial Tanganyika?

options.text: Sisal
Wheat
Rice
Millet

mcq.explanation: Sisal was the leading plantation crop in Tanganyika and was grown mainly for export to make ropes and twine.

mcq.questionText: What is meant by 'land alienation' in the colonial economy?

options.text: Africans being given more fertile land
Taking land from Africans and giving it to settlers and companies
Dividing land equally among all farmers
Leaving land unused for conservation

mcq.explanation: Land alienation was the process of taking fertile land away from Africans and allocating it to European settlers and companies for cash-crop and plantation farming.

mcq.questionText: Why did colonial governments introduce taxes such as the hut tax and poll tax?

options.text: To reward Africans for farming
To force Africans to work for wages in order to earn money
To pay for African schools and hospitals
To encourage Africans to keep more livestock

mcq.explanation: Taxes had to be paid in cash, so Africans were forced to seek wage labour on plantations, mines and settler farms to obtain money.

mcq.questionText: Which labour system involved compelling Africans to work without their consent and often without proper pay?

options.text: Wage labour
Forced labour
Voluntary labour
Family labour

mcq.explanation: Forced labour required Africans to work on colonial projects against their will, often under harsh conditions and with little or no payment.

mcq.questionText: What is migrant labour as practised in the colonial economy?

options.text: Workers who travel long distances from their home areas to work elsewhere
Workers who refuse to leave their villages
Foreign settlers coming to farm in Africa
Children working on family farms

mcq.explanation: Migrant labour involved Africans leaving their home districts, often seasonally, to work on distant plantations, mines or farms.

mcq.questionText: Why did the colonialists build railways and roads in East Africa?

options.text: To develop tourism for Africans
To transport raw materials to the coast for export
To connect African villages for social visits
To replace traditional caravan routes for slavery only

mcq.explanation: Infrastructure such as railways and roads was built mainly to move raw materials from the interior to ports and to bring in manufactured goods.

mcq.questionText: The Central Railway Line in Tanganyika was built by which colonial power?

options.text: Britain
Germany
France
Belgium

mcq.explanation: The Germans built the Central Railway Line from Dar es Salaam towards the interior to ease the transport of cash crops and raw materials.

mcq.questionText: Which group of Africans grew cash crops on their own small farms under the colonial economy?

options.text: Settlers
Peasants
Plantation companies
Colonial soldiers

mcq.explanation: In peasant agriculture, African small-scale farmers were encouraged or forced to grow cash crops such as coffee and cotton on their own land.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following was a major effect of the colonial economy on Africans?

options.text: Africans became rich industrial owners
Loss of fertile land and exploitation of African labour
Equal sharing of profits with Europeans
Total end of all African farming

mcq.explanation: The colonial economy led to land alienation, exploitation of cheap African labour and underdevelopment of African societies.

mcq.questionText: Settler agriculture differed from peasant agriculture mainly because settler farms were:

options.text: Owned by Africans on small plots
Owned by European immigrants on large alienated lands
Owned by the colonial government for free distribution
Worked entirely by machines without labour

mcq.explanation: Settler agriculture was practised by European immigrants who occupied large pieces of alienated land and relied on cheap African labour.

mcq.questionText: Which crop was widely grown by African peasants in the Kilimanjaro area during the colonial period?

options.text: Sisal
Coffee
Rubber
Cocoa

mcq.explanation: The Chagga people around Mount Kilimanjaro became well known for growing coffee as a peasant cash crop during the colonial period.

mcq.questionText: How did the colonial economy contribute to the decline of African traditional industries?

options.text: By improving local craft production
By flooding the market with cheap imported manufactured goods
By banning all forms of trade
By teaching Africans new industrial skills

mcq.explanation: Cheap imported goods from Europe out-competed and destroyed local African crafts and industries such as iron-working and cloth-making.

fib.questionText: The main aim of the colonial economy was to benefit the _____ country rather than the colonised people.
fib.explanation: The metropolitan (mother/colonising) country was the chief beneficiary of the colonial economy.

fib.questionText: The process of taking fertile land from Africans and giving it to settlers is called land _____.
fib.explanation: Land alienation deprived Africans of their best farming and grazing land.

fib.questionText: The leading plantation cash crop grown for export in colonial Tanganyika was _____.
fib.explanation: Sisal was Tanganyika's main plantation crop, used to make ropes and twine.

fib.questionText: Africans who travelled far from their home areas to work on plantations and mines were known as _____ labourers.
fib.explanation: Migrant labourers moved away from their districts, often seasonally, to find work.

fib.questionText: Colonial governments introduced the hut tax and _____ tax to force Africans into wage labour.
fib.explanation: The poll tax was charged per person and, like the hut tax, had to be paid in cash, forcing Africans to seek wage work.

fib.questionText: Railways and roads were built mainly to transport _____ materials from the interior to the coast.
fib.explanation: Infrastructure served to move raw materials for export and bring in manufactured imports.

fib.questionText: Small-scale African farmers who grew cash crops on their own land practised _____ agriculture.
fib.explanation: Peasant agriculture involved Africans producing cash crops on their own small farms.

fib.questionText: European immigrants who occupied large alienated lands to farm cash crops practised _____ agriculture.
fib.explanation: Settler agriculture was carried out by European immigrants on large estates using cheap African labour.

fib.questionText: The system in which Africans were compelled to work against their will, often without pay, was called _____ labour.
fib.explanation: Forced labour was widely used to build roads, railways and to work on settler farms.

fib.questionText: The cheap imported goods from Europe destroyed African local crafts and _____, such as iron-smelting and cloth-making.
fib.explanation: African traditional industries declined because they could not compete with cheap European manufactured imports.

tf.questionText: The colonial economy was mainly developed to benefit African people.
tf.explanation: It was developed mainly to serve the interests of the colonising (metropolitan) country.

tf.questionText: Sisal was an important plantation crop grown for export in colonial Tanganyika.
tf.explanation: Sisal was Tanganyika's leading plantation export crop.

tf.questionText: Land alienation means giving Africans more fertile land to farm.
tf.explanation: Land alienation was the taking away of African land for settlers and companies.

tf.questionText: Taxes such as the hut tax forced Africans to look for wage labour to obtain cash.
tf.explanation: Because taxes had to be paid in money, Africans were pushed into wage labour.

tf.questionText: Railways in East Africa were built mainly to connect African villages for social visits.
tf.explanation: Railways were built mainly to transport raw materials to the coast for export.

tf.questionText: Migrant labour involved Africans leaving their home areas to work on distant plantations and mines.
tf.explanation: Migrant labourers moved far from home, often seasonally, to find work.

tf.questionText: Peasant agriculture was practised by European settlers on large estates.
tf.explanation: Peasant agriculture was practised by African small-scale farmers; large estates belonged to settlers and plantations.

tf.questionText: The Germans built the Central Railway Line in Tanganyika to ease transport of raw materials.
tf.explanation: The Central Railway Line ran from Dar es Salaam into the interior, helping move cash crops and raw materials.

tf.questionText: The colonial economy helped to strengthen African traditional industries.
tf.explanation: It weakened them, as cheap imported goods destroyed local crafts and industries.

tf.questionText: Forced labour was used to build roads and railways during the colonial period.
tf.explanation: Africans were often compelled to provide unpaid or poorly paid labour for colonial infrastructure projects.

summary.correctAnswer: To serve the economic interests of the colonising country
summary.explanation: It supplied raw materials and markets for the metropolitan power.
These were the main ways cash crops were produced in the colonies.
Sisal was grown on large plantations for export.

summary.correctAnswer: Taking fertile land from Africans for settlers and companies
summary.explanation: It left Africans with poorer or smaller pieces of land.

summary.correctAnswer: To force Africans to seek wage labour for cash
summary.explanation: Hut and poll taxes had to be paid in money.

summary.correctAnswer: To transport raw materials to the coast for export
summary.explanation: Infrastructure linked the interior to ports.

summary.correctAnswer: Workers travelling far from home to work elsewhere
summary.explanation: Common in plantations and mining areas.

summary.correctAnswer: Compelling Africans to work against their will
summary.explanation: Used for building roads, railways and on farms.

summary.correctAnswer: Decline due to cheap imported goods
summary.explanation: Local crafts could not compete with European imports.

summary.questionText: Overall effect of the colonial economy on Africans
summary.explanation: Africans lost land and were used as cheap labour.

hoq.questionText: Which combination BEST explains how taxation and land alienation worked together to create a cheap labour force for the colonial economy?

options.text: Taxes gave Africans money while land was returned to them, so they chose to work
Land alienation reduced African farmland while taxes demanded cash, pushing Africans into wage labour
Both policies aimed to develop African-owned industries and trade
Taxes were abolished once enough land was alienated

hoq.explanation: By taking away land, Africans could no longer rely fully on their own farming, and cash taxes forced them to earn money through wage labour on settler farms, plantations and mines.

hoq.questionText: Why is it argued that the colonial economy led to the UNDERDEVELOPMENT of African societies rather than their development?

options.text: Because profits and raw materials flowed out to Europe while African industries and skills were neglected
Because Africans were given full control of railways and mines
Because the colonialists built many universities for Africans
Because all profits were reinvested locally in African villages

hoq.explanation: Wealth and raw materials were exported to Europe while local industries, skills and balanced growth were ignored, leaving African economies dependent and underdeveloped.

hoq.questionText: How did the difference between settler and peasant agriculture affect African farmers in colonies like Tanganyika and Kenya?

options.text: Both systems gave Africans equal access to fertile land and markets
Settler agriculture often took the best land and labour, limiting opportunities for African peasant farmers
Peasant agriculture was banned wherever settlers were present
Settlers grew only food crops while peasants grew all the cash crops

hoq.explanation: Where settler agriculture dominated, the best land was alienated and African labour was directed to settler farms, restricting peasants' land, labour and chances to compete in cash-crop production.
